deep.reconstruction:
This page has no derivation in the computational sense. It is a foundational reflection prompted by Cantor's letters to Hilbert (1897-1899) on 'fertige' (consistent, completed) versus inconsistent multiplicities.

(1) Complaint. Cantor's notion 'fertig' (a totality that can be thought of as completed) is not defined. The more one thinks about it, the worse the defect becomes. Hilbert contrasts two cases. One is supposed to think of the system of all transfinite numbers (alephs) as fertig. Yet one is not supposed to do so for the system of all sets generated from the countable set by the operations M^M (the set of all maps M -> M, the 'Belegung' or covering operation) and S (union/summation).

Implicit step (mine): if that generated system were fertig, one could form its union U. Then U^U would have strictly larger cardinality than U (Cantor's theorem). Yet U^U would itself belong to the system, so U^U is contained in U, which is a contradiction. This is the construction known as 'Hilbert's paradox'. Hilbert's point is that Cantor gives no criterion for why one totality counts as fertig and the other does not.

(2) Proposed way out. Look at the theorems and problems of set theory and first try to formulate them without using the word 'Menge'.
- Easy example: there are as many points on a line as in a square, i.e. |R| = |R^2| (Cantor 1877/78).
- Hard example: the problem whether something lies strictly between the countable and the linear continuum, i.e. whether there is a cardinal k with aleph_0 < k < 2^aleph_0 (Cantor's continuum problem).

(3) Semantic programme. Do not think of something existing behind a concept. The word should only mean that one uses a definite fact fixed earlier.
- Example: an irrational number is a 'Ding' about which one knows that every rational number q receives, with respect to it, a mark > or <. This is a Dedekind cut, read as a labelling of the rationals: for sqrt 2, q gets '<' iff q < 0 or q^2 < 2.
- Exactly this fact should be invoked whenever one speaks of the concept.
- One should avoid speaking of 'the system of all irrationals' as a completed totality.
- One may still state general theorems in which the word 'Ding = Irrationalzahl' occurs, e.g. 'there are infinitely many' or 'sqrt 2 is irrational'. There 'Ding' means only 'any thing of which that property alone can be stated'. This amounts to schematic/free-variable generality instead of quantification over a completed domain.
errors: No mathematical errors. The only issue is conceptual, and it is Hilbert's own point: 'fertig' is undefined.

Possible misreport or deliberate provocation: in his 1897 letter Cantor actually said the totality of all alephs is NOT a completed (consistent) set. If the reading 'soll man sich als fertig denken' is correct, Hilbert is either compressing Cantor's position or setting up a contrast to expose the arbitrariness of the criterion. The reading of 'transfiniten Zahl(en)' is uncertain.

results.what: Doubt about Cantor's notion of 'fertig'; the system of all sets generated from the countable set by M^M and union S cannot be a completed set (Cantor's theorem applied to its union).
results.modern_name: Hilbert's paradox (union/self-map version of Cantor's paradox; inconsistent multiplicities)
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert (unpublished, c. 1897; reported by Zermelo; analysed by Peckhaus & Kahle, Historia Mathematica 2002); related to Cantor's paradox (Cantor letters 1897-99)

results.what: Problem whether a cardinality lies between countable and continuum; judged very hard.

Programme to formulate set theory without the word 'Menge'; concepts as references to previously fixed facts; irrationals as 'Dinge' with respect to which every rational gets a mark > or <; avoid the totality of all irrationals, allow schematic general statements.
results.modern_name: Dedekind cuts plus an early implicit-definition/proto-formalist stance (precursor of the axiomatic method and of finitist free-variable generality)
results.usually_credited_to: Dedekind 1872 for cuts; Hilbert's axiomatic/formalist programme 1899-1920s; discussed by Peckhaus, Kahle, Ewald, Sieg

deep.surprise_reason: This notebook entry belongs to the known material on Hilbert's early reaction to Cantor's letters and 'Hilbert's paradox' (Peckhaus & Kahle 2002). The early, explicit anti-totality, schematic reading of concepts is a nice proto-formalist detail, but it is already documented in the scholarship.
